subject: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal

messages.author: fb40a65bd21dcf6f
messages.subject: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
parts:
The manual says that multi_normal_cholesky is more efficient than multi_normal but what is the relative efficiency of multi_normal_prec to both of these?

Thanks,
John.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
parts:
multi_normal_prec() tends to be faster because you don't have to invert a matrix / solve a system of equations. But that is only for the likelihood. If you are using a multinormal prior, then it is best to post-multiply independent standard normals by the Cholesky factor and shift by the mean vector.

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
parts:
Actually, even multi_normal_prec needs to perform a matrix factorization if Sigma is a parameter to compute the log(det(Sigma)) term.

In general it is best to use the version that is most natural.  If you have an inverse covariance matrix, use multi_normal_prec, if you have (or need) the cholesky factor for other reasons, use multi_normal_cholesky.  If you end up calling multi_normal many times with the same covariance matrix, it is *sometimes* worth computing the Cholesky factorization of Sigma once and using multi_normal_cholesky but not often.

Finally, if you start fiddling to make your models "fast" be sure to actually time things.  Because of the complexity of how Stan works, some seeming optimizations can actually make things much slower.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
parts:
Also, if you can vectorize, it'll help with all three parameterizations.
That way, Stan only has to do the factorization once for all of the outcomes.

So rather than

for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu[n], Sigma);

it's much faster to use:

y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

with more advantage as N grows.

- Bob
